name: Moving the Goalposts
statement: Moving the goalposts means changing the criteria for success partway through, after the original criteria have already been met.
statementAccent: changing the criteria for success partway through
meaning: "Moving the goalposts" describes shifting the standard of proof or success after an opponent has already satisfied the original standard, so the goal stays permanently out of reach. It is a metaphor from goal-based sports, where relocating the goal after play began would be manifestly unfair. As a fallacy, it lets someone reject evidence indefinitely by continually raising the bar.
mechanism: A claim is made with an implicit or stated standard of evidence. When that standard is met, the arguer dismisses the evidence and substitutes a new, usually stricter demand — redefining what would count as success. Because success is redefined only after the fact, the original evidence is never engaged with on its merits.

examples.text: The earliest documented figurative use is a 2 May 1924 House of Commons debate: Labour MP George Hardie said the Liberals, having lost, "wanted to shift the goal posts because they could not play any more."
In September 1987, UK Chancellor Nigel Lawson was quoted saying "I see no reason to move the goalposts at all," showing the idiom in mainstream political use by the late 1980s.

In a 2014 NHL game, goaltender David Leggio deliberately dislodged his own goalpost during a breakaway to stop a certain goal; the incident prompted rule changes, and by 2019 the NHL awarded automatic goals in such cases.

whyItMatters: Spotting this fallacy protects the integrity of debate by requiring that a stated standard be honoured once met, rather than letting endless shifting shield a favoured conclusion from falsification. It is common in pseudoscience, political spin, and workplace bullying, where objectives are redefined so they can never be met.
limits: Raising a standard is not fallacious when new, relevant information genuinely justifies a stricter test, or when the original standard was too weak to establish the claim. Genuine refinement of criteria differs from bad-faith goalpost-shifting meant only to avoid conceding a point.
misreadings: The term is sometimes applied to any change of position, but it properly refers to changing the success criterion after that criterion has been met, not to updating one’s views in light of new evidence.
origin: The phrase is British in origin, a metaphor from goal-based sports; its earliest known figurative use dates to a 1924 House of Commons debate, and it entered widespread use during the 1980s.
